title: How to Slice Garlic Thin for Infused Oils and Toppings
meta_description: Learn how to thinly slice garlic with a mandoline for perfect infused oils and toppings. Step‑by‑step tips, safety tricks, and the best mandoline slicer for res
html:
Getting a paper‑thin slice of garlic is a game‑changer for infused oils, garnish‑ready croutons, and even the occasional pizza topping. The trick? Use a mandoline slicer that lets you dial in a razor‑sharp setting and keep your fingers safe. Below is a practical, no‑fluff guide that walks you through the whole process—from prep to storage—so you can achieve uniform, restaurant‑thin slices every time.

Why a Mandoline Beats a Knife for Thinly Sliced Garlic

When you try to slice garlic with a chef’s knife, the result is usually uneven, and the effort can be frustrating. A mandoline slicer gives you three distinct advantages:

  • Consistency: Adjustable blades guarantee the same thickness on every slice, essential for even flavor release in oil.
  • Speed: One smooth motion produces dozens of slices in seconds, saving you precious prep time.
  • Safety: Hand guards keep your fingertips away from the blade, reducing the risk of nicks and cuts.

For those who love restaurant‑thin results, the Mandoline Slicer is a solid choice. Its adjustable settings and built‑in hand guard make it ideal for garlic, as well as carrots, cucumbers, and even delicate fruits.

Preparing the Garlic for Thin Slicing

Start with fresh, firm heads of garlic. Older cloves become papery and can crumble when you try to slice them.

  1. Separate the cloves: Pull away the papery outer skin, then break the head into individual cloves.
  2. Trim the root end: Use a small knife to cut off the hard, woody tip. This gives the mandoline a clean, flat surface to grip.
  3. Peel the skin: The easiest method is to smash the clove lightly with the flat side of a chef’s knife; the skin will slip off easily.

Once peeled, the cloves are ready for the mandoline. If you’re slicing a lot, you can line a work surface with a large cutting board or a silicone mat to catch stray pieces.

Setting Up Your Mandoline for Thin Garlic Slices

Adjust the blade to the thinnest setting—often labeled “0” or “paper thin.” The Mandoline Slicer offers a clear dial, so you can see exactly where the blade sits. Engage the hand guard before you start; it slides onto the mandoline’s front and provides a stable platform for the garlic clove.

Place the peeled clove on the guard with the flat side down. This orientation helps the blade glide smoothly and prevents the clove from slipping.

Technique: Slicing Garlic Thin with a Mandoline

Now for the actual slicing. Hold the hand guard firmly with one hand and use the other hand to push the clove toward the blade. A gentle, even pressure yields the best results—don’t force the clove, or you’ll risk crushing it instead of slicing.

As you slide the clove across the blade, the mandoline will produce a ribbon of garlic that falls onto your cutting board. If you need a larger batch, repeat the motion, repositioning the clove each time. The key is to keep the clove flat against the guard; any tilt can cause uneven slices or a dangerous slip.

When you’re done, turn off the mandoline (if it’s a model with a built‑in safety lock) and carefully detach the hand guard. Use a brush or a soft brush attachment on your kitchen vacuum to clear any stray bits from the blade.

Using Thinly Sliced Garlic in Infused Oils and Toppings

Thinly sliced garlic dissolves quickly, releasing its aromatic oils without the bitterness that can develop from over‑cooking larger pieces. Here are two quick ways to capitalize on those paper‑thin slices:

  • Garlic‑Infused Olive Oil: Warm 1 cup of extra‑virgin olive oil over low heat, add a handful of thin slices, and let them steep for 10‑15 minutes. Strain and store in a sealed jar for up to a week.
  • Garlic Crisps for Toppings: Toss the slices with a drizzle of oil, spread them on a parchment‑lined sheet, and bake at 350°F for 5‑7 minutes until golden and crisp. Use them to top salads, pastas, or pizza.

Because the slices are so thin, both applications retain a delicate garlic flavor without overwhelming the dish.

Cleaning and Maintaining Your Mandoline Slicer

Proper care extends the life of the blade and keeps the tool safe for future use. After each session:

  1. Disassemble the mandoline according to the manufacturer’s instructions.
  2. Rinse the blade and guard under warm, soapy water. Use a soft brush to remove any clingy garlic bits.
  3. Dry all components thoroughly before re‑assembling. Store the slicer in a drawer with a protective cover or a dedicated slot to avoid accidental contact with other utensils.

Never soak the blade for extended periods; stainless‑steel blades can develop rust if left wet for too long.

FAQ

Can I use a mandoline to slice whole garlic heads?

It’s not recommended. Whole heads are too bulky for the blade and hand guard. Peel and separate the cloves first for safe, even slices.

Do I need a special blade for garlic?

No special blade is required. The standard ultra‑thin blade that comes with the Mandoline Slicer works perfectly for garlic and most other vegetables.

Is the hand guard enough protection for my fingers?

Yes, as long as you keep the guard engaged and follow the recommended slicing technique. Always push the food toward the blade, never pull it away.
